title: Judge the judge
brief: Your scorer is a model, and models have habits. The decision you are making, the availability of reference answers and the cost of a wrong verdict are unspecified. Set up the judge so that a change in score means something.

blocks.text: A judge is an instrument with measurable habits

items.label: Agreement with humans
items.note: GPT-4 reached 85% against 81% among humans in the non-tie setup. Measured on 2023 models.

items.label: Consistency after swapping order
items.note: GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 with the default prompt. Newer judges are likely better, but no measurement was found on 2026-10-13.

items.label: Math grading failures, out of 20
items.note: Default judge, then chain-of-thought, then a reference-guided judge

items.label: Order flipped a ranking
items.note: Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries once answer order changed, with ChatGPT as judge

items.label: Few-shot judge
items.note: GPT-4 consistency gain, at about 4 times the prompt cost

blocks.title: Pick the judge setup
blocks.prompt: Flip the decision, the reference and the stakes. The ranking shows which setup carries the least risk.

options.name: Pairwise with order swap
options.summary: Compare two answers in both orders.

options.name: Reference-guided pass/fail
options.summary: Grade against a known correct answer.

options.name: Calibrated binary judge
options.summary: Pass/fail tuned to an expert's critiques.

rank.why: Absolute scores drift and compress, so close systems tie.

gate.why: Workable with a threshold, though unanchored 1 to 5 scales are noisy.

yes.why: A reference is available and this format does not use it.

no.why: Works with no reference, which is why it is the default.

high.why: Uncalibrated scores are risky when verdicts matter.

rank.why: Pairwise is more reliable for ranking, and swapping removes position bias.

gate.why: It needs a comparison partner, not a threshold.

yes.why: References can be added, but are not required.

no.why: Compares two answers, so no reference is needed.

high.why: Counting only wins that hold in both orders is conservative.

rank.why: Works, though it scores each system alone.

gate.why: Pass/fail against a reference maps cleanly to a threshold.

yes.why: Reference-guided grading cut math failures from 14 to 3 of 20.

no.why: Nothing to guide the judge with.

low.why: Longer prompts cost a little more.

high.why: Strong on verifiable tasks, where errors are checkable.

rank.why: Binary verdicts lose fine ordering, though win counts still rank.

gate.why: Pass/fail with a threshold and written critiques is the OpenAI and Husain advice.

no.why: Anchored by expert critiques instead of references.

low.why: Calibration needs expert time that low stakes do not repay.

high.why: Measured true positive and true negative rates are what high stakes need.

gate.why: Needs a rule for combining verdicts into one threshold.

yes.why: Each judge can use the reference, with no special gain.

no.why: Different families cross-check each other when nothing else anchors them.

high.why: Disagreement between judges flags items for human review.

blocks.takeaway: Rank with pairwise, gate with calibrated pass/fail, and use references wherever the answer is checkable.

blocks.title: The judge calibration loop
blocks.alt: An expert labels a sample, a judge prompt is drafted and run, true positive and true negative rates are computed, disagreements drive prompt refinement until agreement is acceptable, then the judge is frozen and re-checked on a fresh human sample.
blocks.src:
flowchart TB
  L["Expert labels a sample"] --> D["Draft judge prompt"]
  D --> R["Run judge on the sample"]
  R --> M["Compute TPR and TNR"]
  M --> Q{"Agree enough?"}
  Q -->|No| X["Read disagreements, refine prompt"]
  X --> R
  Q -->|Yes| F["Freeze judge version"]
  F --> W["Re-check on a fresh sample"]
blocks.caption: Husain's critique shadowing reached over 90% agreement in three iterations on his example. Report TPR and TNR, not raw agreement, when classes are imbalanced.

items.symptom: The pairwise winner flips when the answer slots swap
items.cause: Position bias: most judges favour the first slot
items.fix: Run both orders and count a win only when it holds both ways. Report the share of inconsistent pairs.

items.cause: Verbosity bias. In the MT-Bench repetitive-list attack, Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 failed 91.3% of the time and GPT-4 8.7%.
items.fix: Control for length, penalize padding in the rubric and test the judge with padded answers.

items.symptom: Your own model scores high on a judge from its own family
items.cause: Self-preference: judges recognize their own outputs and favour them
items.fix: Use a different family from the generator or a panel, and spot check against a human sample.

items.symptom: Agreement is 92% and the judge never flags failures
items.cause: Imbalanced labels, so raw agreement hides a low true negative rate
items.fix: Report TPR and TNR, and keep failure examples in the calibration sample.

items.symptom: A move from 4.2 to 4.4 is celebrated
items.cause: No interval, and an uncalibrated 1 to 5 scale
items.fix: Use binary criteria with a threshold, a paired comparison and a confidence interval before acting.

items.symptom: Scores shift after the judge model is upgraded
items.cause: A different model brings different habits
items.fix: Pin the judge version, recalibrate against the human sample and rerun the baseline whenever the judge changes.

items.title: Go deeper: G-Eval and rubric judges

blocks.md: G-Eval combines chain-of-thought with a form-filling prompt that ends in a score. With GPT-4 it reached a Spearman correlation of 0.514 with humans on summarization, and its authors flag a bias toward LLM-generated text. DeepEval implements it as `GEval` [[r22]] [[r28]].

items.title: Go deeper: more than three biases

blocks.md: The CALM framework quantifies 12 biases in LLM judges, not only position and verbosity [[r44]]. MT-Bench found GPT-4 favoured itself with about a 10% higher win rate and Claude-v1 about 25%, but called the evidence inconclusive [[r21]]. A later study found judges can recognize their own outputs, and self-recognition correlated linearly with self-preference after fine-tuning [[r32]]. Fixes proposed for order effects include Multiple Evidence Calibration, Balanced Position Calibration and human-in-the-loop calibration [[r31]].

items.title: Go deeper: judge cost arithmetic and custom judges

blocks.md: Swapping order doubles the calls, and a few-shot judge costs about 4 times the prompt tokens. OpenAI advises validating agreement against human labels before optimizing cost or latency, asking the judge to reason before it scores, and preferring pairwise comparison or pass/fail for more reliability [[r18]].

In Foundry, `builtin.output_quality` and `builtin.tool_use_quality` batch several criteria into one judge call (preview, 2026-10-13) [[r3]]. A prompt-based custom evaluator (preview) returns JSON with a `result` and a `reason`, which lets you ship a calibrated judge as a first-class evaluator [[r41]].

quiz.q: The stored answers are identical in both runs. Only the slot order changed. Which cause best fits?

code.code:
run 1: prompt B in slot 1 -> B wins 68% of 200 comparisons
run 2: prompt B in slot 2 -> B wins 49% of 200 comparisons

options: Position bias: the judge favours whichever answer sits in slot 1
Verbosity bias: prompt B writes longer answers than prompt A
Self-preference: the judge shares a model family with the generator
Sampling temperature in the generator changed between the two runs
quiz.explain: Only the slot moved, and B's win rate fell from 68% to about chance, so the slot drove the verdict. Verbosity bias and self-preference follow the answer, so B would keep winning after the swap. The generator is not involved because the stored answers were re-judged unchanged. The swap-and-agree rule exists to catch exactly this.

quiz.q: Select the mitigations that research or vendor guidance supports for judge reliability.
options: Run each pair in both orders and count a win only when it holds in both
Give the judge a reference answer on tasks with a checkable solution
Calibrate against pass/fail labels and critiques from one accountable domain expert
Use a judge from the same model family as the generator so that style matches
quiz.explain: Swapping order addresses position bias, and a reference-guided judge cut math failures from 14 to 3 of 20 [[r21]]. Calibrating to one expert's critiques is the critique shadowing method [[r16]]. The fourth option backfires: a judge that recognizes its own family's style favours it, which is self-preference [[r32]].

quiz.q: A judge is checked on 100 items. 90 are truly passing and 10 are truly failing. It labels 88 of the 90 passing items correctly and 3 of the 10 failing items correctly. Treating failing as the negative class, what is its true negative rate, in percent?
quiz.hint: True negative rate = failing items the judge flagged divided by all truly failing items.
quiz.explain: The judge flags 3 of 10 true failures, so the true negative rate is 30%. Raw agreement is (88 + 3) / 100 = 91%, which looks healthy while 7 of 10 real failures slip through. This is why imbalanced classes need TPR and TNR.

quiz.q: You must gate one prompt change against a threshold. A domain expert has one day to give labels and there are no reference answers. Which judge setup fits best?
options: A pointwise 1 to 10 score averaged over the whole set and compared with the last release's average
A pairwise judge comparing the new prompt with the old one, always in the same fixed order, as the gate
A binary pass/fail judge calibrated to the expert's labelled critiques, with a stated threshold
Two pointwise judges from different families whose fine-grained scores are averaged into one gate value
quiz.explain: Gating one system favours pass/fail with a threshold, and the expert's critiques are the input that calibrates it [[r16]] [[r18]]. Averaged 1 to 10 scores are the uncalibrated scale Husain warns against. A fixed-order pairwise judge is exposed to position bias and compares rather than gates. Averaging two fine-grained scores reduces noise a little but leaves the scale uncalibrated.

takeaways: A judge is a model with measurable habits: position, verbosity and self-preference bias.
Swap order, use references where answers are checkable, and calibrate against one accountable expert.
Report true positive and true negative rates, not raw agreement.
Rank two systems with pairwise comparison. Gate one system with calibrated pass/fail.
Pin the judge version and recalibrate when it changes.
